senses.gloss:
andhatāmisra
------------------------------------------
According to the Sāṅkhyadarśana, one of the more well-known systems of Hindu philosophy, there are two types of च्रेअतिओन्: the elemental च्रेअतिओन् and च्रेअतिओन् of बुद्धि. The latter, called pratyaya-sarga, is fourfold: विपर्यय (ignorance), aśakti (incapacity), तुष्टि (contentment) and siddhi (perfection or powers). Andhatā-misra is a subdivision of विपर्यय and is manifested as fear of death or self-destruction. Eighteen varieties of this are mentioned. There are five gross objects of pleasure enjoyed through the five organs of perception (e.g., शब्द or sound by śrotra or ear etc.) and five subtle objects, their counterparts, enjoyed in higher worlds like हेअवेन्. There are also eight सिद्धिस् or powers like अणिमा (capacity to become atomic in size) and so on. The fear that these सिद्धिस् may be lost is अन्धतामिस्र.
In the योग system of पतञ्जलि this is called अभिनिवेश (excessive attachment or clinging to life).
The words tāmisra and अन्धतामिस्र have also been used in the पुराणस् to indicate certain hells into which people committing certain types of heinous crimes and sins (like सुइचिदे, usurping the wealth and women of other people) are cast.

Āndhra
------------------------------------------
Earliest reference to the Āndhras is in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (33.6) where they are mentioned as one of the low-caste groups along with Pulindas, Puṇḍras and Mūtibas. These castes were created by the fifty sons of विश्वामित्र as a result of his curse. The Āndhras were outcastes subsisting on wild animals.
However, आन्ध्र as a country and as a people has found mention in the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and some of the पुराणस्. The country referred to was that between the rivers गोदावरी and Kṛṣṇā.
The आन्ध्र country was part of अशोक’s empire. The political history of an independent आन्ध्र starts with the Śātavāhanas (280 B. C.—A. D. 218). The Kākatīyas (11th to 14th cent. A. D.) were another important dynasty which contri-buted to the cultural development of the आन्ध्र. However it was under the विजय-nagar kings (A. D. 1336—1556) that specta-cular progress was achieved.
